title: The replica that lied
arc: A rider updates their address, then sees the old one on the next screen. Support logs it as a bug; it is a law of physics, or close to it. This week you go underneath every data tool Meridian uses: storage engines, replication and lag, partitioning and hot spots, transactions and isolation, consensus and clocks, exactly-once, and the serving side. By Friday you can explain read-your-writes to support in one sentence and to an interviewer in five.
previously: Why did the rider see their old address right after changing it?
What does a quorum read promise that a single replica does not?
Recall: which isolation level stops a lost update?
Why can a Postgres replication slot fill a disk?
cliff: A rider saw their old address. Bug, or physics?
Two replicas disagree. Which one is right?
Two clocks disagree by 40 milliseconds. Whose event came first?
Surge pricing needs demand per minute, now. Can a nightly batch do that?

scenes.monday: Support escalates: a rider changed their address and the app showed the old one. Dev says "replication lag" and shrugs. Start with why a data engineer needs this.
scenes.midweek: Two services read the same trip and disagree. Build a quorum read with read repair, then compare vector clocks to see which version came first.
scenes.friday: Design a trip store that survives a lost data centre, then read the Postgres lens: MVCC, vacuum and why a replication slot can fill a disk.
